question: Which estate in land gives its holder the largest possible bundle of rights, of potentially infinite duration, freely inheritable and transferable with no conditions attached?
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the highest and most complete form of ownership recognized in real property law. It has unlimited duration, no conditions on use, and passes freely by sale, gift, or inheritance.
source_note: General real property law: freehold estates, fee simple absolute.

question: A deed reads: 'Grantor conveys to the school district so long as the land is used for a public school.' The district stops using the land for school purposes. What is the legal effect?
choice_a: The district keeps title but must pay a penalty
choice_b: Title automatically reverts to the grantor or the grantor's heirs
choice_c: The land escheats to the state
choice_d: Title vests in whoever is currently in possession
explanation: Words of automatic termination such as 'so long as' create a fee simple determinable. The grantor retains a possibility of reverter, and title reverts automatically the instant the stated condition is violated, without any need for legal action.
source_note: General real property law: fee simple determinable and possibility of reverter.

question: A deed states: 'To Buyer, but if the property is ever used to sell alcohol, Grantor reserves the right to re-enter and terminate the estate.' What kind of estate is created, and how does it differ from a fee simple determinable?
choice_a: A fee simple determinable; it terminates automatically
choice_b: A life estate; it ends upon the grantor's death
choice_c: A fee simple subject to a condition subsequent; termination requires the grantor to affirmatively exercise the right of re-entry
choice_d: A leasehold estate; it ends at the expiration of its term
explanation: Because the clause grants the grantor a right of re-entry ('reserves the right to re-enter') rather than triggering an automatic reversion, this is a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent. Unlike a fee simple determinable, title does not revert automatically — the grantor (or successor) must take affirmative action to reclaim the estate.
source_note: General real property law: fee simple subject to a condition subsequent and the power of termination (right of re-entry).

question: Owner O conveys property 'to A for life.' What kind of estate does A hold, and what happens if O dies before A?
choice_a: A leasehold estate; it passes to O's heirs when O dies
choice_b: A fee simple determinable; it ends when O's estate is probated
choice_c: A remainder; A takes possession only after O dies
choice_d: A conventional life estate measured by A's own life; A retains possession until A dies regardless of O's death
explanation: A conventional life estate is measured by the life of the life tenant (A). A's right to possess and use the property continues until A dies, and O's own death has no effect on A's possessory interest.
source_note: General real property law: conventional (ordinary) life estates.

question: Owner O conveys property 'to A for the life of B.' A dies first, while B is still living. What happens to the property?
choice_a: A's interest passes to A's heirs or estate for the remainder of B's life, since the measuring life (B) has not yet ended
choice_b: The estate ends immediately and reverts to O
choice_c: B automatically becomes the new life tenant in fee simple
choice_d: The property escheats to the state
explanation: This is a life estate pur autre vie — measured by the life of a person other than the holder. Because the estate is measured by B's life, not A's, A's death does not end the estate; A's interest for the remaining duration of B's life passes to A's heirs or devisees.
source_note: General real property law: life estate pur autre vie.

question: Owner O conveys property 'to A for life, then to B.' What future interest does B hold?
explanation: A future interest created in a third party (someone other than the original grantor) that becomes possessory when a prior estate ends is called a remainder. Here, B's interest becomes possessory automatically when A's life estate ends.
source_note: General real property law: remainder interests following a life estate.

question: Owner O conveys property 'to A for life' and names no other party to take the property afterward. What interest does O retain?
explanation: When a grantor conveys a life estate without naming a remainderman, the grantor retains a reversion — the right to regain full ownership automatically when the life estate ends.
source_note: General real property law: reversionary interests retained by a grantor.

question: Under the legal doctrine of waste as applied to life estates, which action would most likely expose a life tenant to liability to the remainderman?
choice_a: Collecting and keeping rents generated by the property during the life estate
choice_b: Making ordinary repairs needed to keep the property in good condition
choice_c: Living in the property as a personal residence
choice_d: Demolishing a structure or stripping resources in a way that permanently reduces the property's value
explanation: A life tenant has a duty not to commit waste — that is, not to take actions that permanently damage or diminish the value of the property to the detriment of the remainderman or reversioner. Collecting rents, making normal repairs, and residing on the property are all within the life tenant's ordinary rights.
source_note: General real property law: the doctrine of waste and life tenant obligations.

question: A tenant signs a lease that specifies a definite beginning date and a definite ending date, such as a one-year lease running from June 1 through May 31. What type of leasehold estate is this?
explanation: An estate for years is a leasehold with a fixed, definite beginning and ending date agreed to in advance. Despite its name, it can be for any specific length of time, even less than a year, and it terminates automatically on the stated end date without notice.
source_note: General real property law: leasehold estates — estate (tenancy) for years.

question: A residential tenant pays rent on the first of each month with no signed lease specifying an end date, and the tenancy automatically continues from month to month until either party gives proper notice. What kind of leasehold estate is this?
explanation: A periodic tenancy (such as a month-to-month tenancy) automatically renews for successive equal periods until one party gives the legally required advance notice to terminate.
source_note: General real property law: leasehold estates — periodic tenancy.

question: A landlord allows a friend to occupy a house with no rent, no lease, and no fixed term, and either party may end the arrangement at any time upon proper notice. What type of leasehold interest exists?
explanation: A tenancy at will has no fixed term and continues only as long as both parties agree to it; it can generally be terminated by either party after reasonable statutory notice.
source_note: General real property law: leasehold estates — tenancy at will.

question: A tenant's one-year lease expires, but the tenant remains in possession and continues paying rent without the landlord's consent to a new lease term. What is this tenant's legal status called?
explanation: A tenant who remains in possession ('holds over') after a lease term expires, without the landlord's consent, has a tenancy at sufferance — the lowest form of leasehold interest, essentially a technical trespasser until the landlord either evicts the tenant or accepts rent to create a new tenancy.
source_note: General real property law: leasehold estates — tenancy at sufferance (holdover tenancy).

question: Which characteristic is unique to a joint tenancy and distinguishes it from a tenancy in common?
choice_a: The right of survivorship, under which a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving joint tenant(s)
choice_b: Co-owners may hold unequal percentage shares
choice_c: Each co-owner's interest passes to their heirs upon death
choice_d: Only married couples may hold title this way
explanation: The defining feature of joint tenancy is the right of survivorship: when one joint tenant dies, that owner's interest passes automatically and immediately to the surviving joint tenant(s), bypassing probate and the deceased's will. Tenancy in common has no survivorship right.
source_note: General real property law: joint tenancy and the right of survivorship.

question: To create a valid joint tenancy at common law, which four 'unities' must generally be present at the time the tenancy is formed?
choice_a: Unity of marriage, income, deed, and location
choice_b: Unity of time, title, interest, and possession
choice_c: Unity of survivorship, financing, credit, and title
choice_d: Unity of possession, marriage, purchase price, and heirs
explanation: The traditional common-law 'four unities' required for a valid joint tenancy are unity of time (interests vest at the same time), title (acquired by the same deed or document), interest (equal, undivided shares), and possession (equal right to possess the whole property).
source_note: General real property law: the four unities of joint tenancy.

question: Three owners, A, B, and C, hold title as joint tenants. A sells her interest to D during her lifetime. What is the resulting ownership structure?
choice_a: D becomes a joint tenant with B and C, and all three share survivorship rights equally
choice_b: The joint tenancy is completely destroyed and all three parties become tenants in common
choice_c: D holds an interest as a tenant in common with B and C, while B and C continue to hold their interests as joint tenants with each other
choice_d: D automatically inherits the entire property upon A's later death
explanation: A conveyance by one joint tenant during their lifetime severs the joint tenancy only as to that owner's share. The purchaser (D) takes title as a tenant in common, while the remaining original joint tenants (B and C) continue to hold their unities intact and remain joint tenants with survivorship rights between themselves.
source_note: General real property law: severance of joint tenancy by conveyance.

question: Which statement correctly describes tenancy in common?
choice_a: All co-owners must hold equal ownership shares
choice_b: A deceased co-owner's interest passes to the surviving co-owners automatically
choice_c: It may only be created between married persons
choice_d: Co-owners may hold unequal, undivided interests and each interest passes to that owner's heirs or devisees upon death
explanation: Tenancy in common allows co-owners to hold unequal percentage interests, each of which is a separate, freely transferable and inheritable undivided interest in the whole property. There is no right of survivorship — a deceased tenant in common's share passes according to that owner's will or the laws of intestate succession, not to the other co-owners.
source_note: General real property law: tenancy in common.

question: Which form of concurrent ownership is available only to legally married spouses and generally requires both spouses to join in any conveyance of the property?
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership reserved for married couples, treating husband and wife as a single legal unit. Like joint tenancy it carries a right of survivorship, but it also provides added protection: neither spouse can convey or encumber the property unilaterally, and in many jurisdictions the property is shielded from the debts of only one spouse.
source_note: General real property law: tenancy by the entirety.

question: A married couple purchases a home in a community property state using income earned by either spouse during the marriage. How is this property generally classified?
choice_a: Separate property belonging solely to the spouse whose name is on the deed
choice_b: Community property, owned equally (50/50) by both spouses regardless of whose income paid for it
choice_c: A tenancy in common with unequal shares
choice_d: Trust property held for the benefit of any future children
explanation: In community property states, most assets and income acquired by either spouse during the marriage are considered community property, owned equally by both spouses regardless of which spouse earned the income or whose name appears on the title.
source_note: General real property law: community property ownership.

question: Which of the following is generally classified as separate property, rather than community property, in a community property jurisdiction?
choice_a: Wages earned by either spouse during the marriage
choice_b: A home purchased during the marriage with marital income
choice_c: Property one spouse owned before the marriage, or received individually by gift or inheritance during the marriage
choice_d: Investment income generated from marital earnings
explanation: Separate property generally includes assets a spouse owned before the marriage, along with property acquired individually during the marriage by gift, bequest, or inheritance. Community property instead consists of income and assets earned or acquired jointly during the marriage.
source_note: General real property law: distinction between separate property and community property.

question: In a condominium form of ownership, what best describes the buyer's ownership interest?
choice_a: A leasehold interest in the unit and stock ownership in the building corporation
choice_b: A license to occupy the unit for a fixed number of weeks each year
choice_c: A partnership interest in the entire building
choice_d: Fee simple ownership of the individual unit's airspace, combined with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the common elements
explanation: A condominium owner holds fee simple title to the airspace within their individual unit and, simultaneously, an undivided interest as a tenant in common with the other unit owners in the building's common elements (such as hallways, roof, land, and amenities).
source_note: General real property law: condominium ownership structure.

question: How does ownership in a residential cooperative differ fundamentally from ownership of a condominium unit?
choice_a: A cooperative owner holds shares of stock in the corporation that owns the entire building, plus a proprietary lease to occupy a specific unit — a personal property interest rather than direct real property title
choice_b: A cooperative owner holds fee simple title to their individual unit, exactly like a condominium
choice_c: A cooperative owner has no right to occupy any specific unit
choice_d: There is no legal difference between a cooperative and a condominium
explanation: In a cooperative, a corporation holds title to the entire building. Residents purchase shares of stock in that corporation and receive a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a particular unit. This makes the cooperative owner's interest personal property (stock plus a leasehold right), unlike a condominium owner's direct fee simple title to real property.
source_note: General real property law: cooperative ownership versus condominium ownership.

question: A buyer purchases the right to occupy a vacation unit for one specific week each year, and receives an actual deeded, transferable, inheritable fee interest in that week. What type of ownership is this?
explanation: Timeshares generally take one of two forms. An interval ownership (fee simple) timeshare conveys actual deeded real property title to a specific recurring time interval, which the owner can sell, will, or pass on to heirs. This differs from a right-to-use timeshare, which is merely a contractual license to use the property for a set period that expires and reverts to the developer.
source_note: General real property law: timeshare ownership — fee (interval) ownership versus right-to-use.

question: A vacation club sells buyers the contractual right to use a unit for two weeks each year for 20 years, after which all rights expire and revert to the developer. No deed to real property is ever transferred. What kind of timeshare arrangement is this?
explanation: A right-to-use timeshare grants only a license or contractual right to occupy the property for a defined period and duration; no real property title passes to the purchaser, and the right typically expires and reverts to the developer at the end of the contract term.
source_note: General real property law: right-to-use timeshares.

question: A single individual purchases a property and takes title in their own name alone, with no co-owners. What is this form of ownership called?
explanation: Ownership in severalty means ownership by a single person or single legal entity, severed or separated from ownership by anyone else. Despite the name, it does not involve dividing ownership among multiple parties.
source_note: General real property law: ownership in severalty (sole ownership).

question: Which business ownership structure exposes each owner to unlimited personal liability for the debts and obligations of the business, and allows any one owner to bind the others through actions taken on the business's behalf?
explanation: In a general partnership, every general partner shares unlimited personal liability for partnership debts and obligations, and each partner generally has authority to bind the partnership in dealings with third parties.
source_note: General business law: general partnerships and partner liability.

question: A real estate investment structure includes at least one general partner who manages the venture and bears unlimited liability, and one or more limited partners who invest capital, take no part in day-to-day management, and risk only their investment amount. What is this structure called?
explanation: A limited partnership has two classes of partners: general partner(s), who manage the business and bear unlimited personal liability, and limited partner(s), who are passive investors whose liability is capped at the amount they invested, provided they do not participate in management.
source_note: General business law: limited partnerships.

question: Which characteristic best describes a corporation as a form of business ownership?
choice_a: It has no existence separate from its owners and dissolves whenever an owner dies
choice_b: Each shareholder is personally liable for all corporate debts
choice_c: It is a distinct legal entity that can hold title to property, sue and be sued, exists independently of changes in ownership, and generally limits shareholders' liability to their investment
choice_d: It cannot own real property in its own name
explanation: A corporation is a legal entity separate and distinct from its owners (shareholders). It can own property, enter contracts, and sue or be sued in its own name, has continuity of existence regardless of changes in ownership, and shields shareholders from personal liability beyond their investment.
source_note: General business law: corporations as a form of business ownership.

question: Which business entity is commonly favored for real estate ownership because it combines the limited personal liability of a corporation with the pass-through (single-level) income tax treatment typically associated with a partnership?
explanation: An LLC is often used to hold real estate because its members receive liability protection similar to corporate shareholders, while the entity's income can be taxed on a pass-through basis to the members rather than being subject to separate entity-level (double) taxation like a traditional C corporation.
source_note: General business law: limited liability companies (LLCs) in real estate ownership.

question: An investment trust pools money from many investors to purchase and manage a portfolio of income-producing real estate, and its shares can be bought and sold much like stock. To maintain favorable tax treatment, this type of trust must distribute a large majority of its taxable income to shareholders each year. What is this entity called?
explanation: A REIT allows investors to pool capital to invest in income-producing real estate (or real estate financing) with liquidity similar to owning stock. To qualify for favorable pass-through tax treatment, federal law requires a REIT to distribute at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders annually.
source_note: General business/investment law: real estate investment trusts (REITs).

question: In a land trust, legal title to real property is held by a trustee, while the beneficiary retains the right to control the property, receive income from it, and direct its sale — often while the beneficiary's identity remains confidential in the public record. What is this arrangement most commonly used for?
choice_a: Converting real property into personal property automatically
choice_b: Privacy and estate planning purposes, while the beneficiary retains beneficial control and enjoyment of the property
choice_c: Eliminating all property taxes on the trust property
choice_d: Automatically creating a joint tenancy among all beneficiaries
explanation: A land trust separates legal title (held by the trustee, often as a matter of public record) from beneficial ownership (retained by the beneficiary, who directs the trustee and enjoys the benefits of the property). It is commonly used for privacy and estate planning purposes.
source_note: General property/trust law: land trusts.

question: A group of investors pools capital, typically through a limited partnership or LLC structure, to jointly finance and develop a large real estate project such as a shopping center. What is this common arrangement called?
explanation: A real estate syndication is a pooling of financial resources by multiple investors, usually organized as a limited partnership, LLC, or similar entity, to acquire, develop, or manage real estate that would be difficult for any single investor to finance alone.
source_note: General business law: real estate syndications.

question: A legal description begins 'Commencing at the iron pin at the intersection of Elm Street and 1st Avenue, thence North 200 feet, thence East 150 feet, thence South 200 feet, thence West 150 feet to the point of beginning.' What method of legal description is this?
explanation: Metes and bounds description traces a parcel's boundary using compass directions (bearings) and distances from a defined point of beginning, proceeding around the perimeter of the tract until the description closes back at that same point of beginning.
source_note: General property law: metes and bounds legal descriptions.

question: A valid metes and bounds legal description must satisfy which essential requirement?
choice_a: It must begin and end at the same identifiable point, forming a closed traverse around the parcel
choice_b: It must reference a recorded subdivision plat
choice_c: It must use only township and range coordinates
choice_d: It must be expressed exclusively in acres
explanation: A metes and bounds description must 'close' — that is, the sequence of directions and distances must return exactly to the point of beginning, forming a complete, closed boundary around the parcel. A description that fails to close is legally defective.
source_note: General property law: metes and bounds descriptions must close.

question: Under the U.S. government (rectangular) survey system, a standard township is a square parcel measuring approximately how many miles on each side, and how many sections does it contain?
explanation: Under the rectangular (government) survey system, a township is a roughly 6-mile-by-6-mile square, subdivided into 36 sections, each approximately one square mile (640 acres).
source_note: General property law: government (rectangular) survey system — township and section grid.

question: In the government (rectangular) survey system, township lines and range lines are measured from what two reference lines?
choice_a: The equator and the international date line
choice_b: The nearest county boundary and the nearest state line
choice_c: A principal meridian (running north-south) and a base line (running east-west)
choice_d: A recorded plat and a benchmark elevation
explanation: The rectangular survey system establishes a grid using a principal meridian, a north-south reference line, and a base line, an east-west reference line. Township lines are numbered in tiers north or south of the base line, and range lines are numbered in columns east or west of the principal meridian.
source_note: General property law: government (rectangular) survey system — principal meridians and base lines.

question: A parcel is legally described as 'the NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of Section 12.' Assuming a standard 640-acre section, how many acres does this parcel contain?
explanation: A standard section contains 640 acres. Each successive quarter description divides the prior area by four: the SW 1/4 of the section is 640 / 4 = 160 acres, and the NE 1/4 of that 160-acre quarter is 160 / 4 = 40 acres.
source_note: General property law: government survey aliquot part calculations.

question: A developer subdivides raw land into individual home sites and records a subdivision plat map with the county that assigns each parcel a specific lot number within a numbered block. Deeds for the individual lots then simply reference 'Lot 14, Block 3' of that recorded plat. What method of legal description is this?
explanation: The lot-and-block (recorded plat) method describes property by referring to a specific lot and block number shown on a subdivision plat map that has been surveyed and recorded in the public land records, most commonly used for residential subdivisions.
source_note: General property law: lot-and-block (recorded plat) legal descriptions.

question: A surveyor needs a fixed, permanent point of known location and elevation to accurately tie a new survey into established government or local land records. What is this reference point called?
explanation: A benchmark, or monument, is a permanent, fixed marker of known location and/or elevation set by surveyors, used as a reference point to verify or establish boundaries and elevations in future surveys.
source_note: General property law: survey benchmarks (monuments).
